For this work, we investigated four compositions of the PCM-salt slurry and a control of the salt without PCM particles. For all the PCM cases, we assumed that PCMs occupied 36% by weight of the salt slurry. This limit was provided by PowderMet Inc. The compositions that were investigated include (refer to Table 2 for PCM referenced numbering): 1. Salt-only: Third generation molten salt without PCM particles 2. 3-Tier PCM: Includes all PCMs at equal quantities, i.e., 12% each 3. 2-Tier 50/50 PCM: Includes PCMs 1 and 2 at equal quantities, i.e., 18% each 4. 2-Tier 30/70 PCM: Includes PCMs 1 and 2 at 70% and 30% quantities, i.e., 25.2% and 10.8%, respectively 5. 1-Tier PCM: Includes PCM 1 only Figure 3. Specific heat and change in enthalpy of the five HTFs from 450 °C to 750 °C. Figure 3 presents the specific heat and change in enthalpy for five HTF cases investigated from 450°C to 750°C. The estimate of change in enthalpy was calculated using 450°C as the reference for all cases. From the change in enthalpy, it can be seen the quantity of latent heat added to the salt by the PCMs. The impact of phase change can be observed in Figure 3 as a high specific heat or steep increase in enthalpy occurring over a small temperature range. The 1-tier PCM has the greatest change in enthalpy of all the cases because the PCM 1 heat of fusion is the highest of all the PCMs, and all cases use a constant composition of PCM to salt (i.e., 36% by weight). 13 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nrel.gov/publications. 1.6 HTF Hot Temperature For this work, we varied HTF hot temperature for all PCM salt slurry cases to understand the importance of HTF hot temperature on PHX design and cycle cost. HTF hot temperature was parameterized between 695°C and 755°C using 5°C increments. During some of the PCM cases, specific HTF hot temperatures would result in temperature crossover within the PHX model, which would result in the model failing to solve. This modeling failure could be overcome by increasing either the hot, cold, or both PHX approach temperatures until the temperature crossover no longer occurs. However, for a given HTF hot temperature, increasing the PHX hot approach temperature results in a lower sCO high temperature, which reduces cycle design 2 efficiency. Conversely, increasing the PHX cold approach temperature results in a decreased HTF temperature difference which increases required HTF mass flowrate and decreases TES energy density. In a real heat exchanger, this crossover event would result in the CO and HTF 2 temperature difference decreasing until no heat transfer occurs between the two fluids. This would be a poorly designed PHX because the heat exchange surface area is effectively wasted. Therefore, for the above reasons, the failed cases are omitted in the results.
